EVALUATING ON EBENCH

Benchmark Results

We evaluated GPT-6-Astra across all 26 tasks and 510 episodes in the EBench test-mini suite, and compared its performance with the open-source model results reported on the EBench leaderboard.1

More interestingly, GPT-6-Astra exhibits a distinctly different capability profile from the other evaluated models. We first describe the evaluation setup, then examine these differences through the complete benchmark results.

1. We note that Amapbot Group also submitted evaluation results. Because a reliable model description and supporting references are unavailable, we do not include those results in this report’s analysis.

EXPERIMENT SETUP

Comparing two routes to robot control.

The main evaluation covers the 26 EBench test-mini tasks in nine scene categories: 19 mobile and seven tabletop tasks, spanning household, retail, and industrial settings. Controlled variations change objects, backgrounds, instructions, and their combinations. We report equal-weight task means for complete success (SR) and normalized terminal partial credit (Score), using 510 retained episodes.

Agentic control and learned policies

GPT-6-Astra runs with high reasoning effort. It receives overview and wrist-camera RGB images, end-effector and gripper state, base pose, and the simulator timestep. It requests end-effector poses, gripper and base targets, and action durations; a fixed execution interface carries out those requests. No learned VLA or WAM generates or refines its actions. The agent receives updated observations when a tool call returns, after its requested waypoint sequence has executed. Internally, the interface records execution in chunks of up to eight physics steps; these are transport units, not additional model decisions.

The compared VLA/WAM policies have been trained on the benchmark task types. GPT-6-Astra instead receives one historical demonstration per task. A separate GPT-6-Astra instance running with high reasoning effort reviews one video trajectory from the training set and autonomously selects the keyframes and writes the accompanying prompts. The resulting ICL package contains 10–18 annotated keyframes, operation phases, arm roles, and selected state/action examples. This package is reused across instances, while the model adapts the procedure to live observations without task-specific parameter updates or automatic coordinate replay.

Papers, citations and official GitHub repositories for all compared models.

What is shared—and what is supplied

GPT-6-Astra follows the server’s task-specific physics horizons and live-camera interface. It receives no depth, ground-truth object poses, camera calibration, intermediate scores, or subgoal-completion signals. A common prompt supplies a grasp-verification procedure, including a small test lift; this is guidance provided to the agent, not a strategy it discovered. Each episode starts a fresh model history, and there is no explicit transfer of experience between episodes.

The policy phase has no additional aggregate token, tool-call, or wall-clock cap. If GPT-6-Astra stops before terminal evaluation, the runner holds the robot and advances the simulation to obtain the server result. The leaderboard comparison uses the same task suite and task-macro metrics. Model-specific input and control interfaces are documented in the protocol notes.

A separate test of unseen composition

The POC sits outside the 26-task cohort. Comparison policies are retrained on its atomic skills and familiar objects, but the evaluated task combinations are unseen. No ground-truth (GT) trajectories are available for the composed POC tasks, so evaluation uses zero-shot execution rather than ICL. All systems execute without a test-time demonstration. This separates understanding and composing a new task from robustness within a demonstrated task.

GENERAL ANALYSIS

Three questions behind the results.

01
Where does GPT-6-Astra differ from learned policies?

Mobile manipulation and visual grounding, alongside the precision and completion advantage of specialized policies.

↗02
Where does execution break down?

Contact uncertainty, unfinished stages, and the cost of local retries.

↗03
What new capabilities appear during interaction?

Exploration, recovery, and using the experience of a failed attempt to change the next one.

↗

01 / CAPABILITY DIFFERENCES

A strong mobile profile.
An uneven execution profile.

GPT-6-Astra leads on mobile, short-horizon tasks. Cross-group results reveal where that advantage holds—and where specialized policies remain stronger.

Mobility and horizon change the comparison.

Task-macro success rates across all eight systems. Select a subgroup to inspect its tasks.

Second overall, with sharply different strengths.

GPT-6-Astra ranks first on 9 of 26 tasks and second on five. The first-place count includes four ties: two at positive success rates, and two tasks—bottle and shop—where all eight systems record zero success. Five tasks are outright wins. At the other end, it ranks sixth or seventh on six tasks. These task-level differences convey more than the overall ranking.

02 / FAILURE PATTERNS

Why progress fails
to become completion.

Two recurring patterns organize the failures: getting close without satisfying the contact requirement, and repairing individual actions without completing the whole procedure.

Across 510 episodes, 237 reach complete success. Of the 273 incomplete episodes, 188 receive positive partial credit and 85 score zero. Most failures therefore include scored progress, but the task-level breakdown reveals two different patterns: failing before a scored milestone, or completing intermediate operations without satisfying the final requirement.

Zero-score episodes account for 75% of gear installation, 65% of utensils placement and 50% of glasses packing. In contrast, nut tightening, peg insertion and shop have no zero-score episodes; bottle has 30%. Their low success rates mask different outcome distributions.

The task distributions distinguish failure before a scored milestone from progress that remains unfinished. A zero score does not necessarily mean no physical progress: task-specific scoring rules determine which milestones receive credit. The videos and interaction logs below help locate what actually failed.

The fixed-base gap extends beyond high precision.

On the three fixed-base tasks labelled low or medium precision—frame placement, cup flipping and glasses packing—GPT-6-Astra averages 31.67% success, compared with Qwen-RobotManip’s 91.67%. Cup flipping reaches 10% versus 90%; glasses packing reaches 20% versus 90%. Removing the high-precision tasks therefore does not remove the fixed-base deficit.

Precision labels alone do not explain the capability gap. Depth and contact estimation, object orientation and coordination between the arms are plausible contributors, consistent with the qualitative trajectory analysis. The glasses comparison shows an unresolved folding and closure sequence; the frame ICL case illustrates how a demonstration can supply a better division of labour between the arms. These examples help interpret the statistics without attributing the whole subgroup difference to a single mechanism.

03 / EMERGING AGENT CAPABILITIES

Explore, recover,
and learn from an attempt.

From a local explanation to reusable experience

The apple rollout connects a stated failure diagnosis to a changed action: after identifying a slip during transport, GPT-6-Astra changes its next transport attempt. This is a concrete form of experience use within an episode. The more ambitious possibility is an embodied agent that retains such lessons and uses them to improve later tasks.

That prospect changes what we should evaluate. Beyond final success, useful questions include whether exploration reduces uncertainty, whether a correction repairs the relevant state, and whether an explanation leads to a better next attempt. Recovery can be evaluated as a sequence: detect a disrupted goal, obtain useful evidence, revise the action, restore the goal, and complete the task. Recording opportunities and unsuccessful attempts alongside successes would show when recovery works and what it costs. This evaluation starts fresh histories for each episode; it does not test retained learning across tasks or recursive self-improvement.

04 / SAFETY IN EXECUTION

Executable in simulation.
Safe in the physical world?

A terminal success label does not capture every event along the trajectory. The apple episode succeeds after a loss of grasp; the glasses comparison leaves an obstruction at closure; the coffee-bean episode repeatedly revises contact height without completing the task. These recorded events highlight grasp stability, clearance and contact uncertainty as safety concerns.

CONCLUSION AND INSIGHTS

Conclusion and Insights:
where shall we head to?

Across EBench, GPT-6-Astra handles a wide range of embodied tasks with one annotated demonstration per task. Its performance and recorded behavior reveal a useful combination of task understanding and spatial reasoning: it handles changes in the environment, explores alternative approaches, recovers from errors, and uses experience from an unsuccessful attempt to revise what it does next. These behaviors point toward embodied agents that can adapt their procedures as an interaction unfolds.

Precise alignment and manipulation remain clear execution bottlenecks, with leading specialized policies retaining a substantial advantage on precision-sensitive tasks. The execution logs expose a related control challenge: GPT-6-Astra selects corrections between action batches, while contact and grasp stability can change during a batch. Large EEF corrections and awkward object poses introduce a further concern: a simulated task may permit motions that would be unsafe for real objects or robot hardware. Taken together, these findings motivate four directions for embodied research.

Combine on-device policies with agents

We see complementarity between frontier agents and VLA/WAM or other low-level control policies. GPT-6-Astra’s task interpretation, generalization, and recovery capabilities offer ways to handle unfamiliar states that are difficult for demonstration-trained policies. Conversely, specialized policies can supply responsive execution and precise manipulation within the conditions they have learned. A useful system would let an agent decide when to explore, revise a goal, or recover, while a local controller maintains the fast feedback needed to execute safely and accurately.

The central question is how to couple these capabilities: the agent can specify goals and contact assumptions, while a local controller reports grasp loss, unexpected contact, and primitive completion. Those events provide concrete conditions for interrupting execution and returning control to the agent. RPent, which exposes VLA skills as retryable tools to an agentic planner, offers one concrete direction. Our results motivate evaluating such combinations under scene changes and contact-sensitive tasks; they do not imply that either component should replace the other.

Teach smaller policies to plan, explore, and recover

A second opportunity is to transfer the strong model’s action strategy into smaller on-device policies. GPT-6-Astra can provide more than successful demonstrations: its rollouts include attempts to obtain better observations, diagnoses of failed actions, and changes in approach. These sequences could teach a policy when to inspect, when to retry, and when to abandon an ineffective procedure. A useful training unit would connect the goal, failure state, revised strategy, and observed outcome, retaining unsuccessful corrections as well as successful recovery.

This broadens imitation beyond reproducing trajectories toward intention imitation: learning the relationship between a goal, the observed state, and the choice of a corrective strategy. The challenge is to preserve that relationship across different scenes and embodiments, rather than copy the teacher’s coordinates or its mistakes. Agent-generated exploration could make training data more scalable than human demonstrations alone, provided that transfer quality, safety, and collection cost are verified.

Turn exploratory experience into transferable knowledge and tools

The apple recovery illustrates a small but important loop: identify a failure, summarize a lesson, and change the next attempt. A broader research direction is to turn such experience into reusable skills, contact checks, recovery procedures, or tools that improve the agent and its harness. This is a concrete route to studying recursive self-improvement (RSI) in embodied systems.

The decisive test is whether an acquired lesson improves later execution on held-out tasks—not merely whether the agent can describe it. Can an exploration-derived tool reduce retries or improve completion? Can it help a harness built around a different base model? An experience-derived tool should record its applicable conditions and completion checks, then be frozen and evaluated on new tasks alongside raw-history and no-memory alternatives. Answering these questions would connect within-episode adaptation to cumulative improvement across tasks. Our current evaluation resets episode histories, so it establishes the motivation for this direction rather than demonstrating cross-episode RSI.

Make safety part of the action policy

Task success alone is an insufficient objective for physical deployment. A grasp can be recovered after a drop, yet the drop itself may already have caused damage. Large pose corrections, obstructed closure, and uncertain contact height call for constraints that operate during execution: motion and force limits, clearance and grasp checks, coordinated bimanual control, and the ability to interrupt a hazardous action. An agent must also be able to recognize when its geometric understanding is inadequate and seek a safer observation or assistance.
